newsitem.title: USA: States seek to delay immigrant Food Stamp cutoff.
newsitem.headline: States seek to delay immigrant Food Stamp cutoff.

text.p: Governors across the nation are scrambling to extend Tuesday's deadline for beginning a process that would cut a million legal immigrants off the federal Food Stamps programme.

Worried about the impact on the poor and on their own state's treasuries, 34 states and the District of Columbia will take advantage of an option in the controversial new welfare law that allows them to keep legal residents in the programme for up to four more months, federal officials said.

Without the extension, states would have to start culling legal immigrants from the programme April 1. Even with the reprieve, the law requires all legal immigrants be removed from the rolls by Aug. 22.

The fact most governors want to delay the cutoff is further evidence they find the immigrant provisions of the welfare law too tough and expensive. Many face the prospect of rearranging state budgets to replace lost federal aid.

"States are trying to push the impact back," said Yvette Jackson, deputy administrator of the Agriculture Department's Food Stamp programme. "There are concerns about the severity of cuts affecting legal immigrants and the fact that, for many, there is no other support available."
Advocates for the poor called the governors' decision welcome news, especially since it includes immigrant-heavy states like California, Florida and New York.

But they point out the delay only helps those who were receiving Food Stamps on Aug. 22, 1996, when the welfare law was signed. Legal immigrants who have applied for benefits since that date are not eligible and have been turned away.

"Some of the provisions (of the welfare law) were done with the federal budget in mind, not policy. The impacts are very harsh for people and states know that," said Carrie Lewis, senior policy analyst at the Food Research and Action Centre.
About half the $54.6 billion in six-year savings in the welfare bill comes from denying Food Stamps and disability aid to legal immigrants.
Advocates for the poor filed suit in New York and California last week to block the law, charging that denying benefits to legal immigrants was unconstitutional.
The National Governors' Association earlier this year asked Congress to revisit the issue of aid to immigrants.

Congressional Republicans are considering a block grant to aid heavily hit states -- but argue governors will receive a financial windfall under the welfare law because caseloads are declining faster than expected.

New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani also sued. His city has 135,000 immigrants who would be affected by the Food Stamp cutoff. Under New York's constitution, the state must pick up some of the lost nutrition and disability benefits, at an estimated cost of about $450 million a year.

Florida Democratic Gov. Lawton Chiles last week announced he would extend the Food Stamp deadline, helping an estimated 84,000 legal immigrants in his state. Other states may create their own programmes to make up for Food Stamp cuts.

The White House wants to restore some disability aid to immigrants and delay the Food Stamp-cutoff to Sept 30. An estimated one million legal immigrants will lose Food Stamps, most in California, Texas, New York and Texas.
Under the law, legal immigrants who were receiving Food Stamps on August 22, 1996 are eligible until at least April 1.

Beginning April 1, immigrants lose benefits when their current "certification" expires, but no later than Aug. 22, 1997. States certify Food Stamp recipients periodically to ensure they meet income guidelines.
To avoid the cutoff, some states acted ahead of April 1 to recertify immigrants through Aug 22. The Agriculture Department will also let states extend benefits after April 1 for many immigrants.
